h1: The 8 Best Immersion Blenders Under $200 for Soups, Sauces and Smoothies, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 immersion blenders under $200 compared on attachments, speeds, cordless freedom and brand support, from Braun to Vitamix.
summary: The Braun MQ9187XL MultiQuick 9 is the best immersion blender under $200 for cooks who want one tool with eight attachments. The Breville BSB530XL is the strongest all-in-one processing station, the Vitamix bundle is the pick for brand loyalists, and the KitchenAid Go is the one to buy if you hate cords.
intro: Most people buying an immersion blender think they are buying a blender. They are actually buying a stick, and the stick is where the compromises hide. Under $200 you can get anything from a plain wand that purees soup in a pot to a multi-piece station with a whisk, chopper and beaker, and the mistake is paying for accessories you will never take out of the box.

So this ranking looks at what each unit actually adds. We reviewed eight models from their listings and spec sheets, sorting by attachment count, speed range, cordless or corded design and the brand behind them. Where a listing is thin, we say so plainly and avoid making up wattage or motor figures that were never published.

products.name: Braun MQ9187XL MultiQuick 9 Hand Blender, 8 Attachments
products.verdict: The most capable kit under $200, with eight attachments from a brand that built its name on this tool.
products.description:
The MultiQuick 9 comes with eight attachments, which turns a soup stick into a small kitchen system. The listing leans on Braun's reputation for hand blenders, and the $100 to $200 price puts it near the top of the budget in this guide.

It ranks first because more attachments means the single motor unit replaces a mini chopper, a whisk and a masher, and Braun is a name most cooks trust for this tool. It tops the Breville station because the focus is the blender itself, not a countertop add-on. The tradeoff is storage: eight pieces need a drawer or a box, and you will use only three or four regularly.

Buy it if you cook from scratch and want one motor for many jobs. Skip it if you only puree soup, since a simpler wand does that for less.
pros: Braun's long track record with blenders
products.idealFor: Home cooks who want a complete set of attachments.
products.skipIf: You only puree soup and want something simple.

products.name: Breville BSB530XL All In One Processing Station, Brushed Stainless Steel
products.verdict: A blender wand with a bundle of accessories, packaged as a full processing station.
products.description:
Breville sells the BSB530XL as an all-in-one processing station in brushed stainless steel. The accessories are the point, and the listing positions it as a bundle for people who want to process food, not just blend soup.

It ranks second because the bundle adds chopping and prep capability that a bare stick cannot match, yet it still sits behind the Braun due to fewer clearly stated attachments in the listing. Breville has a reputation for solid build, and the stainless finish suggests it was designed to live on the counter. The tradeoff is footprint and cleaning: more parts mean more to wash after each use.

Buy it if you want to chop onions as well as puree soup. Skip it if you dislike cleaning multiple parts.
cons: More parts to clean each time
Takes more storage than a plain wand
products.idealFor: Cooks who want blending and prep from one purchase.
products.skipIf: You prefer to wash a single shaft after use.

products.name: Vitamix 5-Speed Immersion Blender 3-Piece Bundle, Stainless Steel/Black
products.verdict: Five speeds and a three-piece bundle from the name people trust for blending.
products.description:
The Vitamix bundle offers five speeds, three pieces in the set and the build quality that the brand is known for. It lands in the $100 to $200 bracket, near the cap of this guide.

It ranks third because the five-speed dial gives finer control than a two-button wand, which helps with delicate sauces. The Vitamix name also signals support and spare parts, which matter for a tool that lives hard use. It ranks behind the Braun and Breville because the three pieces are fewer than the eight-piece Braun, and the price is at the upper edge. The tradeoff is paying for the name when similar kits cost less.

Choose it if you already own Vitamix gear or trust the brand. Skip it if you want the most accessories for the money.
cons: Price near the top of the limit
products.idealFor: Vitamix owners who want the same brand in a wand.
products.skipIf: You want the biggest attachment count for the money.

products.name: Breville BSB510XL Control Grip Immersion Blender, Brushed Stainless Steel
products.verdict: A straightforward Breville wand with a grip designed for control, without a bundle of extras.
products.description:
The Control Grip is Breville's plain immersion blender in brushed stainless steel. It does not bundle a station of accessories, and the listing describes it only by the Breville build and name, which is why the details here stay limited.

It ranks fourth because it is the clean choice for a cook who wants a wand and nothing else. The grip in the name refers to how you hold and control the blender, which matters when you are blending hot soup in a deep pot. It trails the station-style models because it offers fewer ways to use the motor. The tradeoff is simplicity: easy storage, but no chopper or whisk to expand it.

Buy it if you puree soup, sauces and smoothies and want little else. Skip it if you want attachments.
pros: Simple wand is easy to store
cons: Costs as much as bundled kits
products.idealFor: Cooks who want a clean wand for soup and sauces.
products.skipIf: You want chopping or whisking attachments.

products.name: KitchenAid Go Cordless Hand Blender w/Accessories, battery included,KHBRV75
products.verdict: A cordless hand blender with accessories and a battery included, for cooks who hate cords.
products.description:
The KitchenAid Go is cordless, with accessories bundled and a battery included. That makes it the only unplugged choice here, and the listing confirms the battery is part of the box.

It ranks fifth because cordless freedom is a genuine benefit: you can move from stove to counter without hunting for an outlet or dragging a cord through a splash zone. The tradeoff is that battery runtime is finite, and the listing gives no run time, so a big batch of soup could outlast a charge. It also sits in the $100 to $200 bracket, a price that competes with stronger corded kits.

Buy it if outlet reach is your main frustration. Skip it if you make large batches or forget to recharge.
pros: No cord to snag or splash
Easy to move around the kitchen
products.idealFor: Cooks who want to blend anywhere, away from an outlet.
products.skipIf: You blend large batches or forget to charge tools.

products.name: KitchenAid Variable Speed Corded Hand Blender with Attachments, KHBV83
products.verdict: A corded KitchenAid with variable speed and attachments, at a mid-range price.
products.description:
The KHBV83 is a corded hand blender with variable speed control and a set of attachments, sold in the $50 to $100 bracket. Variable speed lets you ramp up gradually, which reduces splatter when you start in a pot.

It ranks sixth because the corded model is more affordable than the cordless KitchenAid, with no battery to manage. It lands behind the Braun and Breville because the listing is vague on the number and type of attachments. The tradeoff is the cord: you give up the freedom of the Go but gain unlimited run time, which is the better trade for big batches.

Choose it if you want KitchenAid styling and variable control. Skip it if you want a wider attachment set.
pros: Unlimited run time while plugged in
cons: Cord limits where you can work
products.idealFor: Cooks who want variable speed on a mid-range budget.
products.skipIf: You want a long list of attachments.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 7 3-in-1 Immersion Blender & Food Processor
products.verdict: A 3-in-1 Braun that blends and processes, in the $50 to $100 bracket.
products.description:
The MultiQuick 7 is a 3-in-1 immersion blender and food processor from Braun, with accessories included. Its $50 to $100 price makes it one of the gentler options for a tight budget.

It ranks seventh because the 3-in-1 concept adds chopping to blending at a modest price, but the MultiQuick 9 gives you far more for a bit more money. Braun's build name carries over, so it feels like a fair step up from a bare-bones wand. The tradeoff is that you will probably outgrow three functions if you cook a lot.

Buy it if you want a Braun without paying for eight attachments. Skip it if you want the widest toolkit.
pros: Blends and chops from one motor
Braun brand at a lower price
Easier to store than the 8-piece kit
products.idealFor: Casual cooks who want Braun blending and light chopping.
products.skipIf: You want eight attachments in one kit.

products.name: Ninja Immersion Blender & Whisk, 4 Speeds, 4oz Cup, Deep Navy, CI201ND
products.verdict: A four-speed Ninja with a whisk and small cup, aimed at light everyday blending.
products.description:
The Ninja CI201ND has four speeds, a whisk attachment and a 4 ounce cup, in Deep Navy. It is priced in the $50 to $100 bracket, among the cheaper options here.

It ranks last because the 4 ounce cup suggests small tasks, like a single serving of sauce or a bit of dressing, and the listing says little else. The whisk is useful for cream and eggs, and four speeds are enough for most sauces. The tradeoff is that you are buying a lighter-duty tool, not a system, and the brand has less hand-blender pedigree than Braun or Breville.

Choose it if you blend small portions and want color and a whisk. Skip it if you want a sturdier kit.
products.idealFor: Light users who blend small portions.
products.skipIf: You cook large batches of soup.

methodology.title: Attachment value
methodology.description: We counted the pieces in each kit and asked which ones a home cook actually reaches for, since extras only matter if they get used.

methodology.title: Speed control
methodology.description: Variable-speed dials, 5-speed and 4-speed designs were compared for how well they limit splatter and handle delicate sauces.

methodology.title: Cord or cordless
methodology.description: Corded run time was weighed against cordless freedom, including battery inclusion and the lack of stated runtimes.

methodology.title: Brand and support
methodology.description: Braun, Breville, Vitamix, KitchenAid and Ninja were compared on build reputation and the likelihood of finding spare parts.

methodology.title: Value under $200
methodology.description: Features were set against the $50 to $100 and $100 to $200 price brackets, with nothing over the cap considered.

whatMatters.detail: A blending shaft is the core, but whisks, choppers and beakers add flexibility. Count only what you would pull from the drawer weekly. A kit with eight pieces is wasted if you only ever make soup, so match the list to your cooking.

Variable speed or multiple speed settings let you start slow to avoid splashing. A five-speed or variable dial gives finer control than a two-setting model. On the listing, look for speed counts or the word variable.

A corded blender runs as long as you need, while a cordless unit trades run time for freedom. Battery run time is rarely listed, which is a risk for large batches. If you blend big pots, a corded model is the safer pick.

The shaft is what goes into the pot, and a guard around the blade protects non-stick cookware from scratches. Stainless shafts hold up better than plastic ones. Check whether the listing describes the guard or only the motor.
Detachable shafts are easier to wash and may be dishwasher safe. A kit with many pieces needs a drawer or a box. Think about where it will live before you buy a station-style set.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A long shaft, a blade guard and stable power. Corded designs let you puree a full pot without a battery running out.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Breville Control Grip and the Braun MultiQuick 9 are the strongest soup tools here, with the Braun adding extra attachments.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cook often and want attachments that replace other gadgets. The Braun MQ9187XL and Breville BSB530XL repay the spend.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You make soup a few times a year. The Braun MultiQuick 7 or Ninja is enough.

faq.q: Can I use an immersion blender in a non-stick pot?
faq.a: Yes, but look for a blade guard and keep the blade off the pot floor. Without a guard, the blades can scratch the surface. Check the listing for a guard before using it in coated cookware.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake when buying one?
faq.a: Paying for attachments you will never use. A plain wand handles soup, sauces and smoothies. Add chopper or whisk pieces only if you will pull them out regularly.

faq.q: Is the Braun MultiQuick 9 worth it over the MultiQuick 7?
faq.a: For frequent cooks, yes. Eight attachments replace a chopper, whisk and masher. If you blend now and then, the 3-in-1 MultiQuick 7 costs less and covers the basics.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Snap the shaft onto the motor until it clicks, plug in, and submerge the blade before starting. Begin on the lowest speed to avoid splashing. For cordless models, charge the battery fully first.
Detach the shaft, rinse it right after use and wash with warm soapy water. Never submerge the motor unit. Check the manual before putting any part in the dishwasher.

faq.q: Can it replace a countertop blender?
faq.a: Not fully. It handles soup, sauces and light smoothies, but ice crushing and large batches suit a jar blender better. Many cooks keep both.

finalTake: The Braun MQ9187XL MultiQuick 9 is the best immersion blender under $200, with eight attachments and a long track record behind it. The Breville BSB530XL suits cooks who want a processing station, and the Vitamix bundle is for those who trust the name. The KitchenAid Go is the only cordless choice, and the Braun MultiQuick 7 is the better budget kit. Decide how many attachments you will really use before you buy.
